extracted.intended_audience: educators, curriculum designers, policymakers, and media-literacy advocates (K-12 and after-school program designers)
extracted.subtask_description: A curriculum/framework chapter describing what educators should teach about digital and media literacies: core skills, social competencies, ethical reasoning, and pedagogical strategies to address the participation gap, transparency problem, and ethics challenges in participatory culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access must be coupled with education
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply passing out technology is not enough; expanding access to computers will help only if free connectivity is coupled with educational initiatives to help youths and adults learn how to use those tools effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: municipal Wi-Fi or free networks (Philadelphia, EPS) are valuable but must be paired with programs that teach skills and provide support. Access alone leaves a participation gap where some youth benefit fully and others cannot produce or distribute media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation gap — ensure equal access to skills and experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure every child has access to the skills and experiences needed to be a full participant in the social, cultural, economic, and political future of society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core questions to address: access to skills/experiences; ability to articulate how media shapes perceptions; socialization into emerging ethical standards. Beware that classroom attempts to equalize access can strip advanced students of opportunities; remedial approaches must not limit richer learning for advanced youths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency problem — teach critical examination of media
rubrics_metrics.description: Young people are often limited in their ability to examine media themselves; they can take game or site representations at face value and lack the vocabulary to critique how media constructs meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach students to read media as constructed texts with aesthetic norms, genre conventions, ideological biases, and invisible commercial influences. Use examples (games like SimCity, SimLife; Schrier and Squire studies) to demonstrate that students may test 'what if' hypotheses but still fail to critique representation. Train students to evaluate format/design credibility and to distinguish professional from amateur materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics challenge — socialize emerging ethical standards
rubrics_metrics.description: In participatory culture the line between consumers and producers blurs and established ethical norms are often absent; students need to become reflective about ethical choices and their impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because online communities lack unified watchdogs, media education should encourage questioning and working through ethical dilemmas rather than only providing fixed answers. Use high-school journalism experiences as partial models; acknowledge that online contexts (games, pseudonymous spaces) complicate norms and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twenty-first century literacy (NMC) — abilities beyond access
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Media Consortium defines 21st-century literacy as abilities where aural, visual, and digital literacies overlap: understand power of images/sounds, recognize and use that power, manipulate/transform digital media, distribute them pervasively, and adapt them to new forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modify the NMC definition: (1) textual literacy remains central and should not be discarded; (2) new media literacies should be considered social skills (not merely technical abilities). Emphasize both expressive/manipulative capacities and distributive/adaptive practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual (traditional) literacy remains central
rubrics_metrics.description: Before students can engage with participatory culture they must be able to read and write; new literacies expand rather than replace traditional textual skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat new literacies as building on, not substituting for, reading/writing competencies. Use blogging and other online venues to provide practice and feedback that strengthen core literacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need research competencies: accessing books and articles, taking notes, integrating secondary sources, assessing reliability of data, reading maps and charts, interpreting scientific visualizations, distinguishing fact/opinion, and constructing arguments with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Librarians should be reconceived as information facilitators who help students search online/offline and cultivate good searching and evaluation strategies. Traditional research skills gain importance when students venture beyond curated collections into the open web.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical skills (but not the whole of literacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need practical technical abilities: logging on, searching, using programs, focusing cameras, editing footage, and some basic programming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce media literacy to technical training (analogy: penmanship vs. composition). Technologies change rapidly, so avoid trying to codify a fixed set of tools; focus on transferable technical/problem-solving capabilities rather than specific software.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand media representations and production contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must grasp how media representations structure perceptions, the economic and cultural contexts of media production and circulation, the motives and goals that shape media content, and alternatives outside commercial mainstream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach critical understanding of media as a powerful social, economic, political, and cultural institution. Include analysis of branding/advertising integration (e.g., Neopets) and how commercial interests influence search results and visibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: New social skills and cultural competencies
rubrics_metrics.description: New media literacies are social skills built through collaboration and networking: working within social networks, pooling knowledge (collective intelligence), negotiating across cultural differences, and reconciling conflicting data into coherent pictures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate collaborative activities, long-distance collaborations, and contributions to large-scale communities (fan lists, blogs) into curricula. Emphasize teamwork and the capacity to contribute expertise within diverse groups—skills increasingly demanded in workplaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play as a core mode of learning/problem solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Play is the capacity to experiment with surroundings as a form of problem solving: it motivates learning, allows role-taking, trial-and-error, lowers stakes for failure, and sustains deep engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use games and playful activities to cultivate sustained attention and willingness to persevere ('grind') for payoff. Examples: baseball card collecting fostering literacy/math/geography; game designers' accounts of engagement and problem-solving. Recognize play itself as a skill to teach, not merely a motivational tool for other content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate new literacies into curriculum through cross-disciplinary activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools should integrate new knowledge cultures into everyday teaching via group work and long-distance collaborations, using a range of activities across disciplines and after-school programs to foster these skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide illustrative activities (not exhaustive) that are appropriate to the content being taught. Treat the list of suggested activities as provocations for systematic and creative curriculum design rather than fixed prescriptions.
